target: US, Netherlands and other states seen as backing Israel
concentration_evidence: Arab producers supplied roughly half of world oil exports, but a smaller share of US imports. This is borderline with high if world exports are used.
substitutability_evidence: Non-Arab producers (Iran, Venezuela, Nigeria) and oil companies redirecting cargoes covered part of the gap, but spare capacity was thin.
time_to_replace_evidence: Building new US and allied supply (Alaska, North Sea) took until the late 1970s, and US import dependence kept rising.
cohesion_evidence: 4 members (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Libya, Iraq) were needed to reach about 80% of Arab output. The figures are approximate, and Iraq did not join the production cuts.
dependence_on_target_evidence: Saudi Arabia relied on the US for security, even though the US took a small share of Arab oil exports. This follows the "take the higher of markets or security" rule, but it is group-level and mixed.
state_control_evidence: Producer governments set production levels and ordered the cuts, even where foreign firms operated the fields.

concentration_evidence: The founding members held a large share of world copper **exports**, but far less of world output, because the US and Canada were big producers outside the group.
substitutability_evidence: Copper was a commodity with many producers outside CIPEC, plus scrap and aluminium substitution.
time_to_replace_evidence: Importers could lean on the US, Canada and others, and new mines take several years. With substitutability high, this matters less.
cohesion_evidence: 3 members (Chile, Zambia, Zaire) made up about 80% of the group's output. The figures are approximate.
dependence_on_target_evidence: Copper was most of export earnings for Zambia and Chile, and the industrialised importers were the main markets.
state_control_evidence: Nationalisation was under way when CIPEC was founded (Zaire 1967, Chile's "Chileanisation" from 1967, Zambia 1969), but was not complete in 1967.

concentration_evidence: The producer members (Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and others) held most but not all non-communist output. Bolivia and Brazil were outside.
substitutability_evidence: Aluminium and plastics replaced tinplate in many uses, and non-member producers were expanding.
time_to_replace_evidence: Buyers never had to build their own supply, because the market was in surplus. The US strategic stockpile was existing inventory, not new supply, and opening new mines takes several years.
cohesion_evidence: 3 producers (Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand) made up about 80% of members' output. The figures are approximate.
dependence_on_target_evidence: Tin was an important but not dominant export for the main members, for example Malaysia, whose exports had diversified.
state_control_evidence: The council could set export quotas, and some producers were state-owned (for example, Indonesia's PT Timah), but much mining was private.
scored_by: Claude draft, changed by Andrew (time_to_replace low to medium)

concentration_evidence: China produced the vast majority of the world's rare earths, and supplied about 90% of Japan's imports.
substitutability_evidence: No other producer operated at scale in 2010. Mountain Pass in the US was closed, and Lynas was not yet producing.
time_to_replace_evidence: Lynas began shipping in 2012–13, and Japan cut its dependence substantially within a few years.
cohesion_evidence: Chinese output was spread across many firms, including small and illegal miners. Under the count rule this scores low, even though the state controlled exports (see state control).
dependence_on_target_evidence: Japan took well over 30% of China's rare-earth exports, probably about half or more. It imported about 23,300 t from China in 2010, against roughly 35,000 t of Chinese exports in January–November 2010. This is a rough estimate from two sources that may count products differently. Rare earths were a tiny part of China's economy, so this market-share measure may overstate China's real dependence on Japan.
state_control_evidence: The government set export quotas and licences and controlled customs clearance.

concentration_evidence: Japan supplied about 90% of the fluorinated polyimide and photoresist used by Korean chipmakers, and about 70% of their hydrogen fluoride.
substitutability_evidence: Hydrogen fluoride could be sourced elsewhere or made locally after quality testing. Leading-edge photoresists had few non-Japanese makers. The RIETI study found substitution happened only for hydrogen fluoride.
time_to_replace_evidence: Korean hydrogen fluoride production scaled up within about 1–2 years, but resists and polyimide took longer. Boundary of low and medium for hydrogen fluoride.
cohesion_evidence: Across the three chemicals, 4 or more Japanese firms were involved (for example Stella Chemifa and Morita for hydrogen fluoride; JSR, Tokyo Ohka and Shin-Etsu for resists). Per chemical it would be 2–3.
dependence_on_target_evidence: Korea was a major customer for these Japanese chemicals, because its chipmakers are among the world's biggest buyers. There was no security dependence on Korea.
state_control_evidence: METI's licensing powers were used, and in practice slowed exports, but the producers are private firms. One could argue high, because the government showed it could restrict exports at will.
